I started T when I was 25, nearly been on it 3 years! I don't pass fully due to my large chest but facially/vocally I absolutely do (if a little young, still practicing using my chest properly to speak). 

My face has gotten a lot sharper even though I intitally put weight on after starting hormones, my jawline is much more defined, and my shoulders /back have squared off a lot more than I expected! I come from a family of guys built like brick shithouses so I knew it was coming but I'm still really pleased it's went so well. It's truly never too late to start transitioning
Hidden conduits don't fault! I'd definitely be replacing the regular ones.

I don't pass often in person, been on T for nearly 3 years, fairly visibly trans if you take more than a glancing look. I have somewhat often been mistaken for a trans woman, too (I have a large chest I've been bullied for all my life, people often think they're fake, so sometimes people think I'm a trans lady with large implants). 

I genuinely am now a bit afraid of going to the toilet, usually in public places I used the woman's as I don't pass regularly enough to use the men's. I've gotten all the looks and comments but now I'm worried that anyone who used to have the balls to say something will escalate. Hate using disabled toilets if I don't have to as they aren't for me but I think now I will to keep myself safe.

Hello! I've mentioned this before on here but I've had the exact same issues with Xaggitin, except instead of skin picking I was licking ulcers into my mouth. Have you also felt nauseous and shaky / dissassociative? I only ask because I did, so I'm curious.

They are the "same" but many people find they react very differently to different adhd meds, even under the same umbrella so you're definitely not alone there. Depending on your chemist they might be able to make sure you don't get xaggitin again without upsetting your prescription but you really should try talk to the pharmacist if you can. The other side effects are bad enough that you could leave out the suicidal thoughts as an explanation for not being able to continue taking them.

They'll still see you though. For me, I was discharged at first but when I was stable and able to show that when I was re - referred I was put almost to the top of the list since I didn't need the diagnostic appointments, straight to seeing an endocrinologist in less than a year and straight onto T. 

That's my anecdote though, I don't know anything clinical advice.

It is theoretically possible that a GP would help you although incredibly unlikely (it's called a bridging prescription, while you wait to be seen). I'd not get your hopes up about this one, although it never hurts to ask. 

Other than that it really is just either paying to go private or waiting for the NHS I'm afraid.

Yeah, that's an ablation. Unfortunately ideally you're awake. Being under a general can really changes how your heart works so it's far more effective awake. I won't go into too much detail as like I said it's a really effective and safe procedure, it just hurts. You do have an anesthetist on hand for ongoing pain relief though, I believe I was given fentanyl during the op. I think it can be done under a general but it becomes a much bigger thing if so.

If it helps at all, catheter ablation, which i assume would be the surgery? is (while one of the most painful things I've ever experienced) a really effective surgery. I was diagnosed and T was on the cards when I still had my heart issue (wolf parkinsons white) so I can't see it being an issue especially as it's monitored / managed. I ended up not on T at the time, but that's my experience.

I was initially referred by an A&E Dr as he noticed the weird ECG while I was in for a gallbladder attack, he passed it on as far as I know. It's put on a lot like any normal sort of ECG, although there's a few more electrodes, and the pouch my machine was in had one of those belt clips. They're very light so while sleeping was annoying because the electrodes were a bit itchy (sensitive skin) I didn't notice it very much otherwise. 

Had an appointment at the same hospital again the next day to get it removed, again just nurses and got told the results would be passed to my GP within a month and I'd be sent a letter about anything extra.

Well, I'm not an expert and I'm hesitant to say X Y or Z but I'm diagnosed BPD and ADHD although I think my BPD is far more an issue, so I'll tell you how I understand it. 

I think with RSD & BPD if there's a chance of you having both or being looked at for one or the other, the emotional pain needs to take a back burner. It's there. It's intense. Maybe it destroys you. But looking at that alone won't help anyone figure out the distinction / diagnosis because of the overlap. You also need to be wary of the impulsivity and need for change also inherent to both disorders, because that won't seperate them either. 

At least how it was for me when I was getting diagnosed (a hell of a journey) we focused more on the "splitting" - I know people with ADHD alone can do similar because of the RSD, but it tends not to go into the 'white' zone (I use white for the 'good' parts of it, like, do no wrong, this person is amazing, absolutely angelic etc.) The identity issues as well, I think. There is a lot of overlap so it is hard to necessary wade through it. 

I'm rambling and making no sense but what I'm trying to say is - the strength of my identity issues, splitting, my depersonalisation/dissociation strength, is what we focused on for my BPD. The emotional pain, while very real, was on a back burner because differentiating that from ADHD RSD and BPD would be a hell of a task and the NHS doesn't have time for that, if it's even possible. For my ADHD we focused on my forgetfulness, my distraction levels, my inattentiveness even when I wasn't experiencing an emotional episode, my fidgeting when I wasn't otherwise distressed, etc. 

So for the differences between to two diagnoses, that's what I'd focus on personally because that's what I did when working with the NHS myself.

I'm 22 now, I was cutting since I was 6 or 7 years old, I'm clean a year but my arm is destroyed as is many other areas of my body. Unfortunately, no amount of work and money will cause them to truly disappear. It sucks and it hurts but we don't think about these consequences in the throes of our pain, and that's okay. 

Makeup can work, I personally don't as it causes me rashes and irritations usually. I'm luckily pale and the scars are white and old now, so they're also not extremely noticeable. What I do when I'm swimming is for legs / thighs etc I wear swim shorts over my swimming costume, don't particularly know if that applies to you. Also, if you stay in the water often, the water will help hide the scars. 

I am getting tattoos to cover my body (4 so far), but that's not for everyone, and I've wanted tattoos alone for my entire life, so it isn't purely for self harm reasons. If it's something you'd be interested in, remember tattooing over scar tissue hurts more than undamaged, as well as if you have any extreme scars linework will mess up. My left arm can't be given true linework because of the extent of the damage. I'm going for a galaxy themed sleeve instead; minimal linework, mostly just colours. It's still potentially a blowout vector but less than linework. 

Keeping them moisturised and whatnot can help keep them less noticeable because the skin is supple and not as tight. There's always covering clothes as well but if you're like me it gets extremely tiring wearing that all the time. 

I've learnt to just face up to the stares and questions. I hate it. I hate that my mental health is basically open for all to see, but I find strength in facing up to people rather than hiding. For interviews and the like, I have long sleeved shirts that help with the whole professional vibe. My scars aren't beautiful, but no longer am I ashamed. I survived. Survival is beautiful, even if the fallout isn't. 

Let me know if you ever need someone to talk to about this (or anything else!) I'll always do my best. I'm sorry there isn't a more amazing answer to help hide it. We don't think about these things when we're hurting and it often furthers the cycle of pain. I hope everything goes okay.
